newsitem.title: INDIA: Amnesty concerned over Kashmir poll rights abuses.
newsitem.headline: Amnesty concerned over Kashmir poll rights abuses.

text.p: Amnesty International on Friday expressed concern at the lack of election observers and possible rights abuses in India's troubled Jammu and Kashmir state when local assembly polls start at the weekend.
The London-based human rights group said abuses "could reach a new peak" during the voting that begins on Saturday.

It said it had urged India to "take adequate measures to ensure that human rights defenders, including journalists, can carry out their activities without fear for their lives and safety, and to ensure that no one is compelled by violent means or the threat of violence to cast their votes."
An Amnesty news release was received by Reuters in New Delhi.

More than 20,000 people have been killed since a rebellion began in northern Jammu and Kashmir in 1990. Dozens of separatist groups are fighting either for independence or merger with neighbouring Pakistan.
The state assembly elections, over four days ending on September 30, are being held for the first time in nine years. New Delhi clamped the state under direct rule in 1990.

Amnesty said prominent citizens, human rights activists, journalists and political leaders had been at risk there before and during general elections in May, when the state chose six representatives to the lower house of parliament in New Delhi.

"The state citizen's basic rights are at stake again -- the presence of international elections observers, which could inhibit potential perpetrators from carrying out abuses, has been explicitly ruled out by government authorities," it said.
Some 200,000 Indian security officers fanned out across Kashmir on Friday ahead of polling on Saturday in 26 of the 87 constituencies in the Himalayan state.

"Many residents complained that during the last elections they were caught between militant groups threatening to punish people who dared to vote and the army together with the so-called renegades threatening to punish people who did not," Amnesty said.
The government denied that people had been coerced to vote.
